items.title: 68113_Barney Bigard oral history interview
items.q: We was working at Tom Anderson's for quite a while, just he and I, a duet

ctx.x: Had you known Joe Oliver in New

No. Oh, they were before my time. Well, he heard about me through -- Luis Russell left the band and he went to join King Oliver in Chicago. And then, the funny part, when I got to Chicago -- you see, Albert Nicholas went to Chicago. He left the group. We was working at Tom Anderson's for quite a while, just he and I, a duet, and the trumpet and -- but he didn't tell the man -- he was a Sneaky Pete -- he didn't tell the man he was going to leave, you know, because the man's business turned to bad and the man had…

So I got laid off. And the week I got laid off, that's when Albert took off for Chicago. So he left, and the boss was so angry that he didn't tell him that he was going to leave because he would never have fired me, you know. So he told the guys to go to my house and tell me to come back to work. I said, "I wouldn't come back to work for nothing in the world." So the guys told him I wouldn't come back to work.

items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, 1969-07-25
items.q: Right. It was Albert Nicholas and Paul Barberin.

ctx.x: Hi Bill, this is Floyd Levin in Los Angeles. This is the 25th of July 1969 and shortly I expect Barney Begard over, at which time I will supply the questions and hopefully he'll come up with some of the answers to help you on your quest for information about Jelly Roll Morton. Okay, we've just played the Victor Trio session, Barney. I assume that you have some memories about that session. Yeah, I was really surprised. I thought I played more than I do now. That's going back, what, 40 years? Yes, it is. Could you…
. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. That's okay. You can cut that off. One. Two. You see, if you count and then pick back the notes up, it screws you up. Yeah. ¶ Thank you.

items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, Early 1970s
items.q: And we had two good clarinetists in there, Albert Nicholas and Darnell Howard.

ctx.x: What was it that inspired you to go into music, Marnie Begard?

Me? Well, I wanted to, truthfully, I wanted to be a trumpet player. Really? And, uh, because, and then I could whistle good. So the, the, the old folks, you know, they said, well, the sun is too much wind. You can't blow that kind of horses. I want to try the clarinet. So, uh, I said, okay. So, uh, I said, okay. So, my uncle was a fiddle player, Emil Begard. A fiddle player? Yeah. He used to lead a band. He used to lead Kid Overs band into that. Uh-huh. And, uh, Baby Daz was the clarinetist. And in those, those…

Now you're talking about these marching bands, uh, the bands of New Orleans, you know, going to the funeral and, uh, other occasions and all. Who were some of the people that you might have, uh, marched with? Was Louis Armstrong along with you at the time?

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: And then formed a little group of my own. With Barney B. Godd on tenor we were learning in Saxton.

ctx.x: Can you tell us something about your training and taking lessons and so on?

Well, I started taking lessons around 9 years of age with my uncle, Wooden Joe Nicholas. He was my big influence on this jazz scene. And later on, I went to Papa Teo and took lessons with him for about a couple of years. Then Lorenzo Teo, his son. And finished up with him until around 1915. Then I started to go pro. My first gigs around New Orleans was with the Maple Leaf Band. Then Buddy Petite's Band. When Jimmy Noon left to go to Chicago, I played with Buddy Petite and several other bands around New Orleans.…
